title: 22. Interview: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
summary: Interview Q&A for IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What does "shared responsibility" mean in IaaS, and where exactly is the line drawn?
**Answer:** Shared responsibility is the contractual split of operational accountability between cloud provider and customer. In IaaS, the line is drawn at the hypervisor. The provider is responsible for everything physical: the data center, power, cooling, the physical host, the network cabling, and the hypervisor itself. The customer is responsible for everything above: the guest operating system, kernel patching, middleware, runtime, application code, and the data inside the application. This is fundamentally different from PaaS, where the provider also owns the OS and runtime, and from SaaS, where the provider owns the application too. The practical consequence is that an IaaS customer must run their own patch management, vulnerability scanning, and OS hardening — a CVE in the Linux kernel is the customer's problem, not the provider's. AWS's 2017 S3 outage and the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability were both cases where customers discovered, painfully, that the shared responsibility line meant they had to patch their own EC2 AMIs even though AWS had patched the underlying infrastructure.

**Visual:**
```
Provider:  data center | host | network | hypervisor
Customer:  guest OS | middleware | runtime | app | data
                       ^
                       shared responsibility line (the hypervisor)
```

### Q2. Why is API-first provisioning considered a defining property of IaaS, and what does it enable?
**Answer:** API-first provisioning means every IaaS resource — instance, volume, network, firewall rule — is created, modified, and destroyed via a programmatic API call rather than a purchase order. This unlocks three capabilities that are impossible on bare metal. First, elasticity: an auto-scaling group can call `RunInstances` to add capacity in seconds when load spikes, and terminate instances when it subsides. Second, infrastructure as code: Terraform or CloudFormation templates define the entire fleet declaratively, so environments are reproducible, version-controlled, and reviewable. Third, chaos engineering: Netflix's Chaos Monkey terminates random EC2 instances in production precisely because the API can replace them within minutes. Netflix's migration onto AWS in 2008 was motivated not by cost but by the elasticity ceiling of their own data centers — they could not procure and rack servers fast enough to keep up with subscriber growth. The API turned infrastructure provisioning from a months-long procurement cycle into a seconds-long programmatic operation.

**Visual:**
```
Bare metal:   requisition -> wait 6 weeks -> rack -> cable -> deploy
IaaS API:     RunInstances(count=100)  -->  100 VMs in <30 sec
              Enables: autoscaling, IaC, chaos eng, blue-green, canary
```

### Q3. Explain the IaaS billing model and why it gave rise to FinOps as a discipline.
**Answer:** IaaS billing is metered to the second for compute, GB-month for storage, and GB for egress. AWS moved from hourly to per-second billing in 2017, and Azure and GCP followed. This means cost is a continuous function of architecture — a misconfigured auto-scaling group can burn a million dollars in a weekend, and the team will not notice until the invoice arrives. Pinterest publicly described spending eight figures annually on AWS before disciplined rightsizing cut it dramatically. FinOps emerged as a discipline to bring finance-grade cost accountability to cloud spend: forecasting monthly burn, attributing cost to teams via tags, identifying idle resources, purchasing reserved capacity or savings plans for steady-state workloads, and alerting on anomalous spend. The discipline exists because, unlike a purchased server whose marginal cost is zero once bought, every IaaS second costs money whether you use it or not. Cost becomes an architectural property of the system, not a procurement afterthought.

**Visual:**
```
On-prem server:  $10K upfront, $0 marginal thereafter
IaaS instance:   $0 marginal in steady state but $0.10/hr forever
                  -> 24x7 m5.xlarge = ~$1,000/yr
                  -> 1,000 instances left on by accident = $1M/yr
```

### Q4. What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), and why is it foundational to IaaS networking?
**Answer:** A VPC is a software-defined, logically isolated section of the cloud provider's network where the customer launches resources in subnets they define. It gives the customer full control over IP addressing, routing tables, internet gateways, NAT gateways, and security group firewalls — essentially recreating the network architecture of a physical data center in software. The reason it is foundational is that it is the unit of network isolation and trust. Typical patterns put load balancers in public subnets reachable from the internet, application servers in private subnets reachable only from the load balancer, and databases in isolated subnets reachable only from the application. Instagram's migration to AWS in 2014 used exactly this three-tier VPC layout, allowing them to scale from 30 million to hundreds of millions of users without buying hardware. Without VPCs, every instance would be internet-facing by default — a security posture no enterprise could accept. VPCs make IaaS networking safe enough for production workloads.

**Visual:**
```
VPC 10.0.0.0/16
  +-- public subnet 10.0.1.0/24   <- ALB (internet-facing)
  +-- private subnet 10.0.2.0/24  <- app servers (only ALB can reach)
  +-- data subnet 10.0.3.0/24     <- databases (only app servers can reach)

Security groups enforce: ALB:443 <- 0.0.0.0/0
                        App:8080 <- ALB
                         DB:5432 <- App
```

### Q5. Compare IaaS to bare metal and to PaaS along the dimensions of control, responsibility, and elasticity.
**Answer:** Bare metal gives maximum control — you own the hardware, choose the kernel, even modify firmware — and maximum responsibility: you replace failed disks, manage data center power, and wait weeks to add capacity. Elasticity is effectively zero because procurement is slow. IaaS preserves most of the control (root on the guest OS, custom kernel modules, any runtime) while pushing physical responsibility to the provider, and unlocks massive elasticity via APIs — Netflix runs hundreds of thousands of EC2 instances with hand-tuned kernels. PaaS goes further: the provider owns the OS and runtime, the customer ships only application code, which means less control (no custom kernel, limited runtime versions) but less responsibility (no patching, no scaling configuration). Heroku is the canonical PaaS. The right choice depends on workload: video encoding with custom CPU tuning wants IaaS; a CRUD web app for a startup is faster on PaaS; a database with strict latency requirements might still need bare metal.

**Visual:**
```
                Control   Responsibility   Elasticity
Bare metal      max       max              none (weeks)
IaaS            high      high             high (seconds)
PaaS            low       low              high (seconds, managed)
SaaS            none      none             n/a (provider's problem)
```

### Q6. What are the main risks of an IaaS-first strategy, and how do mature teams mitigate them?
**Answer:** The first risk is operational burden: every EC2 instance needs patching, monitoring, scaling, and backup — work that PaaS or serverless eliminates. Mitigation is to build golden AMIs with Packer, automate patching via SSM or Ansible, and use managed services (RDS instead of self-hosted Postgres) wherever the team does not need IaaS-level control. The second risk is cost explosion: a forgotten dev instance or an over-provisioned ASG can drain the annual budget in weeks. Mitigation is mandatory tagging, automated rightsizing recommendations, spend anomaly alerts, and reserved capacity for steady-state workloads. The third risk is security misconfiguration — publicly exposed S3 buckets, security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 — which causes the majority of cloud breaches. Mitigation is infrastructure-as-code reviews, AWS Config rules, and tools like Cloud Custodian that enforce policy. The fourth risk is vendor lock-in: deep use of provider-specific services (Lambda, DynamoDB) makes migration painful. Mitigation is to keep stateless application code portable and accept lock-in only at the data layer where the cost-benefit justifies it.

**Visual:**
```
Risk                Mitigation
ops burden          golden AMI (Packer) + SSM patching + managed svcs
cost explosion      mandatory tags + spend alerts + reserved capacity
security misconfig  IaC reviews + AWS Config + Cloud Custodian
vendor lock-in      keep stateless code portable; lock in at data layer
```

### Q7. How do auto-scaling groups work in IaaS, and what are their typical scaling policies?
**Answer:** An auto-scaling group (ASG) is a managed controller that maintains a target number of EC2 instances across one or more availability zones, automatically launching replacements when instances fail or terminate and adjusting the count based on load. The ASG is configured with a launch template (AMI, instance type, SSH key, security groups, user-data script), a min/max/desired count, and one or more scaling policies. The two canonical policy types are target-tracking, which adjusts the count to keep a metric like average CPU at 50%, and step-scaling, which adds N instances when CPU exceeds 70% for 5 minutes and removes M when it drops below 30%. More sophisticated setups use predictive scaling, which uses historical load to pre-warm capacity before the daily traffic peak. Netflix's streaming fleet runs hundreds of ASGs across regions, each with custom CloudWatch alarms tied to playback start latency — the metric that actually matters to users, not raw CPU. The ASG is what makes disposable-instance architectures viable: instances are cattle, not pets.

**Visual:**
```
ASG (min=3, desired=6, max=20) across 3 AZs
  AZ-a: i-aaa, i-aab        \
  AZ-b: i-baa, i-bab          } target: avg CPU = 50%
  AZ-c: i-caa, i-cab        /
CPU > 70% for 5m -> +2 instances (cooldown 300s)
CPU < 30% for 10m -> -1 instance
Chaos Monkey kills i-aaa -> ASG launches i-aac within 2 min
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your startup has been running on AWS EC2 for two years and the monthly bill just crossed $500K. The CFO wants a 30% cut. What is your plan?
**Answer:** A 30% cut on a $500K/month bill is $1.8M annually saved, achievable through four levers in priority order. First, rightsizing: most EC2 fleets are 30–50% over-provisioned because engineers pick the instance type they know rather than the one the workload needs. Pull CPU and memory utilization from CloudWatch for two weeks, identify instances below 20% utilization, and downsize them — typically a 15–25% saving with no performance impact. Second, purchase commitments: convert steady-state workloads to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, which yield 30–72% discounts versus on-demand for 1- or 3-year commitments. Third, kill waste: scan for idle EBS volumes, unattached Elastic IPs, oversized NAT gateways, and forgotten dev environments running 24/7 — typically 5–10% of bill. Fourth, architect for cheaper building blocks: replace self-hosted PostgreSQL on EC2 with RDS, move infrequently accessed S3 objects to Glacier, replace some EC2 workers with Spot Instances at 70–90% discount for batch workloads. Pinterest's public 2018 cost optimization described exactly this playbook yielding 40%+ savings.

**Visual:**
```
$500K/mo  -> rightsizing (-15%)  -> $425K
          -> reservations (-25%) -> $320K
          -> kill waste (-5%)    -> $300K
          -> spot for batch (-5%) -> $285K
Total: -43%, target -30% achieved
```

### Q2. You are designing an e-commerce platform for a flash-sale event where traffic will spike 50x for 30 minutes. How do you architect the IaaS layer?
**Answer:** A 50x spike in 30 minutes is a classic flash-sale pattern (think Amazon Prime Day or a Ticketmaster on-sale), and the architecture must be pre-warmed, not reactive. First, run a pre-warm: scale the ASG to expected peak capacity 15 minutes before the sale starts, because booting instances and warming application caches takes 3–5 minutes per instance — too slow if you wait for the spike to hit. Second, use Application Load Balancers with sufficient idle capacity pre-provisioned; ALBs scale automatically but with a delay, so pre-warming avoids the 502 storm. Third, over-provision database read replicas and connection pools — the database is usually the first bottleneck. Fourth, put a CDN (CloudFront) in front of all static and semi-static content so the EC2 fleet only handles dynamic requests. Fifth, configure auto-scaling with aggressive step policies: add 20% capacity when CPU exceeds 60% for 2 minutes, not 5. Sixth, use Circuit Breakers and queue-based load leveling to shed load gracefully if capacity is exceeded — better to show a "please wait" page than to cascade-fail the database. Seventh, run a load test simulating the 50x spike the day before, using distributed load generators. Amazon's own Prime Day architecture follows exactly this pattern.

**Visual:**
```
T-15m:  ASG pre-warmed to expected peak (200 instances)
T-0:    sale opens, ALB + CloudFront absorb initial burst
T+2m:   CPU>60%, step policy adds 20% capacity
T+10m:  DB read replicas at 80%, queue absorbs overflow
T+30m:  sale ends, ASG slowly scales back over 30 min
```

### Q3. Your security team discovers an EC2 instance was exposed with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 for six months. How do you respond?
**Answer:** This is a security incident with potential data-breach implications, so the response is structured as containment, investigation, remediation, and prevention. First, containment: immediately restrict the security group to only known corporate CIDR blocks or remove the SSH rule entirely (use SSM Session Manager for access going forward). Do not terminate the instance yet — forensic evidence lives on its disk. Second, investigation: capture a memory dump and an EBS snapshot, then analyze for compromise indicators — unexpected cron jobs, unauthorized SSH keys in `authorized_keys`, unfamiliar processes, outbound connections to suspicious IPs. Review CloudTrail for any API calls made with stolen credentials from that instance. Third, remediation: if compromise is confirmed, rotate all credentials the instance could access (IAM role, database passwords, API keys) and replace the instance from a known-clean AMI. Fourth, prevention: enforce infrastructure-as-code so security groups are code-reviewed; deploy AWS Config rules that flag any `0.0.0.0/0` on port 22; require SSM Session Manager instead of SSH; run automated scanners like Prowler that alert on drift. Capital One's 2019 breach, which exposed 100M+ records, started from exactly this kind of misconfiguration.

**Visual:**
```
1. Contain:  restrict SG immediately, snapshot disk
2. Investigate: memory dump, CloudTrail, IOCs
3. Remediate: rotate creds, replace from clean AMI
4. Prevent:  IaC-only SGs, AWS Config rule, SSM not SSH
```

### Q4. You need to migrate 200 self-hosted PostgreSQL servers from on-prem to IaaS with minimal downtime. How do you design the migration?
**Answer:** A 200-database migration with minimal downtime requires a phased, replication-based approach rather than a lift-and-shift cutover. First, inventory each database: version, size, dependencies, RPO/RTO, and traffic patterns — group them into migration waves by criticality. Second, set up the target: provision RDS Postgres instances (or EC2 if you need OS-level control) in the appropriate VPC subnets, with matching versions and parameter groups. Third, establish logical replication from each on-prem primary to its cloud replica using PostgreSQL's native logical replication or a tool like AWS DMS — this keeps the cloud replica continuously up-to-date while the source stays live. Fourth, validate: run shadow reads against the replica and compare results to the primary; measure replication lag and ensure it stays under a second. Fifth, cutover per database: pause writes briefly (or use a feature flag), let replication drain, promote the replica to primary, repoint DNS, and resume writes. Total downtime per database: seconds to minutes. Sixth, run both in parallel for a week with rollback DNS ready, then decommission the on-prem source. The AWS Database Migration Service exists precisely to automate this pattern, and most large migrations (like Geico's 2020 cloud move) follow this phased replication approach.

**Visual:**
```
on-prem primary  --logical replication-->  cloud replica
        |                                       |
   live traffic                            shadow reads
        |                                       |
        v                                       v
   cutover window: pause writes, drain lag, promote replica, flip DNS
   downtime per DB: ~30 sec
```

### Q5. A customer reports that their EC2-based application is slow during peak hours. CPU is at 40%, but latency spikes to 5 seconds. What do you investigate?
**Answer:** Low CPU with high latency is a classic bottleneck-elsewhere pattern — the EC2 instance is not the limit, something it depends on is. First, check the database: connection pool exhaustion is the most common culprit. If each request opens a fresh DB connection instead of pooling, the pool maxes out and requests queue. Look at CloudWatch for DB connections, slow queries, and replica lag. Second, check downstream services: a single slow dependency can stall request handlers even when CPU is idle — open a trace in your APM (Datadog, X-Ray) and look for the slowest span. Third, check thread pool and event loop saturation: in Python or Node.js, a single slow downstream call blocks the entire event loop or thread pool, making the instance appear idle while requests pile up. Fourth, check network: if the instance is in a different AZ from its database, cross-AZ latency plus a chatty protocol adds up; check `AWS/EC2` network metrics and TCP retransmits. Fifth, check garbage collection or memory pressure: high GC pauses look exactly like latency spikes with low CPU. Netflix's performance team routinely finds that 80% of "slow EC2" tickets are actually database or downstream service issues masquerading as application latency.

**Visual:**
```
App CPU 40% but latency 5s  -->  bottleneck is NOT the instance
Check:
  DB: connections? slow queries? replica lag?
  Downstream: trace for slowest span
  Thread/event loop: blocked by one slow call?
  Network: cross-AZ? retransmits?
  GC: long pauses?
```

### Q6. You are asked to design a multi-region active-active architecture on IaaS for a global SaaS. What are the key decisions?
**Answer:** Active-active multi-region is the highest-tier availability pattern, used by Netflix, Facebook, and the largest SaaS platforms, and it carries significant complexity. The first decision is data replication: each region must have a writable copy of the data, which means either a multi-master database (CockroachDB, Spanner, DynamoDB Global Tables) or application-level conflict resolution. The trade-off is between strong consistency (hard, slow, limits multi-region writes) and eventual consistency (fast but conflict-prone). The second decision is traffic routing: a global DNS service (Route 53, Cloudflare) routes users to the nearest region based on latency, health checks, and geography. The third decision is failover: if one region fails, traffic must shift to the others within minutes — this requires health checks at multiple layers (instance, ALB, region) and pre-tested runbooks. The fourth decision is statelessness: application instances must be stateless so any user can be served by any region; session state must live in a globally replicated store. The fifth decision is cost: running two full copies of production doubles the bill, so the business case must justify it. Netflix's active-active architecture across three AWS regions is the textbook reference; their 2017 us-east-1 outage proved the design works because streaming continued uninterrupted from other regions.

**Visual:**
```
              Global DNS (Route 53 latency + health)
              /                  |                  \
         us-east-1           eu-west-1          ap-southeast-1
         app + DB  <---replication--->  app + DB  <---replication--->  app + DB
              \                  |                  /
               -> all regions writable, async replication
               -> one region fails, DNS sheds traffic in 60s
```

### Q7. Your team is debating whether to use EC2 with self-managed Kubernetes or to move to a managed PaaS. How do you frame the decision?
**Answer:** The decision hinges on three questions: what level of control do you actually need, what is your team's operational maturity, and what is the cost of the operations you would outsource. EC2 with self-managed Kubernetes gives maximum control — you can tune every kubelet flag, run any CNI, pin any Kubernetes version — but it requires a dedicated platform team to patch, upgrade, monitor, and recover the control plane. Real-world cost: a 4-person platform team is roughly $1M/year fully loaded, before infrastructure. A managed Kubernetes service (EKS, GKE, AKS) removes the control plane burden but still requires node pool management and CNI/CSI choices. A PaaS like App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, or Heroku removes the cluster entirely — you ship code, the platform runs it. The decision framework: if your workload needs custom kernel modules, GPU tuning, or unusual runtime versions, you need IaaS. If you need to run a heterogeneous fleet of services with shared networking policy, managed Kubernetes is the sweet spot. If you are a small team shipping a CRUD app, PaaS will get you to market months faster. Spotify's early use of EC2 with custom orchestration and their later move to Google's managed services is a well-documented example of the trade-off playing out over time.

**Visual:**
```
Control vs Ops burden:
  EC2 + self-managed k8s   high control, high ops (4-person platform team)
  EKS/GKE/AKS              medium control, medium ops (1-2 SREs)
  PaaS (App Engine/Heroku) low control, low ops (ship code, done)

Pick IaaS if:   custom kernel, GPU, runtime not supported by PaaS
Pick k8s if:    heterogeneous fleet, shared networking, team > 10
Pick PaaS if:   small team, CRUD app, time-to-market matters
```
